1. The frames show a comparison of two "piles" of wealth, one for buying a home and one for renting and investing, set against a street of identical houses. The title is "Two piles, one street." The source line cites FHFA (house prices), BLS (rent or inflation data), Freddie Mac (mortgage rates) and K. R. French/CRSP (stock returns). A footer says "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. The title fades in over the first two frames while only the street of houses is visible. From frame 3 on, a wall of vertical bars rises up behind the houses, like a time-series chart. It starts high on the left, sags to a low in the middle, climbs to a bumpy peak on the right, and then levels off slightly. In frames 5 and 6 a gap or dark notch opens in the left-center of the bars. The bars look to be drawn in two overlapping shades, which would be the two piles. I can't tell from the picture which shade is which, and there are no axis labels or numbers.

3. It seems to mean that the outcome of buying versus renting and investing depends on when you start. Across the historical range the gap between the two piles swells, shrinks, and shifts, so no single result applies to every period. The dark notch may mark a stretch where the two came out about equal or where data is missing. I can't be sure of that from the image.

4. A viewer would take away only a mild lesson: history doesn't give one answer, so the result depends on timing and on the data sources used. The footer warns that this is not a forecast. The animation doesn't tell the viewer to rent or to buy.

5. Advice from the animation itself: none. The picture and text suggested only that the comparison is historical and US-only. The "timing matters" takeaway in answer 4 is my own reading of the shape of the bars.
